title: Celsus’s heroes weighed
source_text: Ἐπεὶ ουν ἀναπέμπει ἡμᾶς ἐπὶ τὸν Ἡρακλέα, ἀπομνημονεύματα λόγων αὐτοῦ ἡμῖν παραστησάτω καὶ περὶ τῆς παρ᾿ Ὀμφάλῃ ἀσέμνου δουλείας αὐτοῦ ἀπολογησάσθω, δεικνύτω δὲ εἰ θείας τιμῆς ἄξιος ἦν ὁ τοῦ γεωργοῦ βίᾳ καὶ λῃστρικῶς τὸν βοῦν λαβὼν καὶ καταθοινησάμενος καὶ ἡσθεὶς ἐφ᾿ οἷς ἐκεῖνος καταρώμενος ἔλεγε πρὸς αὐτὸν ἐσθίοντα· ὡς καὶ μέχρι τοῦδε ἱστορεῖσθαι τὸν Ἡρακλέος δαίμονα λαμβάνειν μετὰ τῶν ἀρῶν τὴν θυσίαν. καλεῖ δ᾿ ἡμᾶς ἐπὶ τὴν περὶ Ἀσκληπιοῦ ταυτολογίαν, προειρηκότας καὶ περὶ αὐτοῦ. ἀλλ᾿ ἡμεῖς ἐκείνοις ἀρκούμεθα. τί δὲ καὶ θαυμάσας Ὀρφέως ὁμολογουμένως φησὶν αὐτὸν ὁσίῳ χρησάμενον πνεύματι καλῶς βεβιωκέναι; θαυμάζω δὲ εἰ μὴ καὶ Κέλσος διὰ μὲν τὴν πρὸς ἡμᾶς φιλονεικίαν, καὶ ἵνα Ἰησοῦν ἐξευτελίσῃ, νῦν ὑμνεῖ Ὀρφέα, ὅτε δ᾿ ἐνετύγχανεν· αὐτοῦ τοῖς ὡς περὶ θεῶν ἀσεβέσι μύθοις, οὐκ ἀπεστρέφετο τὰ ποιήματα ὡς μᾶλλον καὶ τῶν Ὁμήρου ἄξια ἐκβάλλεσθαι τῆς καλῆς πολιτείας· καὶ γὰρ πολλῷ χείρονα περὶ τῶν νομιζομένων εἶπε θεῶν Ὀρφεὺς ἢ Ὅμηρος. γενναῖος μὲν οὖν ὁ Ἀνάξαρχος, λέγων τῷ τῆς Κύπρου τυράννῳ Ἀριστοκρέοντι· „πτίσσε, πτίσσε τὸν Ἀναξάρχου θύλακον“· μονογενὲς δὲ τοῦτο περὶ Ἀναξάρχου ἴσασι θαυμαζόμενον Ἕλληνες, ἐφ᾿ ᾧ εἰ καὶ, ὡς Κέλσος, ἀξίως ἐχρῆν τινας σέβειν ἄνθρωπον δι᾿ ἀρετὴν, οὐκ ἦν εὔλογον ἀναγορεύεσθαι τὸν Ἀνάξαρχον θεόν. καὶ ἐπὶ Ἐπίκτητον δὲ ἡμᾶς ἀναπέμπει, θαυμάσας τὸ εὐγενῶς μὲν αὐτῷ λελεγμένον, οὐ μὴν ὥστε παραβληθῆναι αὐτοῦ τὸν ἐπὶ τῇ κατάξει τοῦ σκέλους λόγον τοῖς παραδόξοις τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἔργοις ἀπιστουμένοις ὑπὸ Κέλσου καὶ λόγοις, διὰ τὸ καὶ δυνάμει λελέχθαι θείᾳ μέχρι δεῦρο ἐπιστρέφοντας οὐ τῶν ἁπλουστέρων τινὰς μόνον ἀλλὰ καὶ πολλοὺς τῶν συνετωτέρων.
pass_a_gloss: Since then he sends us back (ἀναπέμπω) to Heracles, let him present (παρίστημι) to us memoirs (ἀπομνημονεύματα) of his words, and let him defend (ἀπολογέομαι) concerning his unseemly (ἄσεμνος) slavery (δουλεία) with Omphale, and let him show whether worthy of divine honour (τιμή) was the one who with force (βία) and robber-like (λῃστρικῶς) took the farmer's (γεωργός) ox and feasted on it (καταθοινάομαι) and was pleased (ἥδομαι) at what that one, cursing (καταράομαι), said to him eating; so that even until now it is reported (ἱστορέω) that the daemon (δαίμων) of Heracles receives the sacrifice with curses (ἀραί). And he calls us to the repetition (ταυτολογία) about Asclepius, having spoken before also about him; but we are content (ἀρκέομαι) with those things. And admiring what of Orpheus does he say that he admittedly, having used a holy spirit, lived well (καλῶς βιόω)? I wonder (θαυμάζω) if Celsus too, on account of rivalry (φιλονεικία) toward us and so that he may cheapen (ἐξευτελίζω) Jesus, now hymns (ὑμνέω) Orpheus, but when he came upon (ἐντυγχάνω) his myths impious (ἀσεβής) as concerning gods, did not turn away from (ἀποστρέφομαι) the poems (ποιήματα) as worthy even more than those of Homer to be cast out (ἐκβάλλω) of the fine constitution (πολιτεία); for Orpheus said much worse things than Homer about the reputed gods. Noble (γενναῖος) then was Anaxarchus, saying to the tyrant of Cyprus Aristocreon: 'pound, pound the bag of Anaxarchus'; but this single (μονογενής) thing about Anaxarchus the Greeks know as admired, on which, even if, as Celsus [says], some ought worthily (ἀξίως) to revere (σέβω) a man through virtue (ἀρετή), it was not reasonable (εὔλογος) for Anaxarchus to be proclaimed (ἀναγορεύω) a god. And to Epictetus too he sends us back, having admired what was nobly (εὐγενῶς) said by him, not however so that his word (λόγος) at the breaking (κάταξις) of his leg be compared (παραβάλλω) with the marvellous (παράδοξος) works of Jesus disbelieved (ἀπιστέω) by Celsus, and words, because of having been spoken with divine power (δύναμις) until now turning (ἐπιστρέφω) not only some of the simpler (ἁπλοῦς) but also many of the more intelligent (συνετός).
pass_b_english: Since, then, he sends us back to Heracles, let him set before us records of Heracles’ sayings, and let him defend his unseemly slavery in the house of Omphale. Let him show whether divine honour was due to the one who took the farmer’s ox by force, like a robber, feasted on it, and enjoyed the curses the farmer called down on him as he ate; so that even to this day the demon of Heracles is said to receive its sacrifice with curses. He also calls us to repeat ourselves about Asclepius, though we have already spoken about him; but we are content with what we said there.

And what did he admire in Orpheus, that he says that he “by common consent had a holy spirit” and lived a good life? I should be surprised if Celsus too, who now sings the praises of Orpheus out of rivalry with us and in order to belittle Jesus, did not turn away from his poems when he came upon his impious myths about the gods, as deserving to be banished from the good state even more than the poems of Homer (Plato, Republic 398a, 607a). For Orpheus said far worse things than Homer about the so-called gods.

Anaxarchus, to be sure, was noble when he said to Aristocreon, the tyrant of Cyprus, “Pound, pound the bag of Anaxarchus.” But this is the one thing about Anaxarchus that the Greeks know and admire; and even if, as Celsus holds, some people ought rightly to revere a man for his virtue, it would not have been reasonable, on the strength of this, to proclaim Anaxarchus a god.

He also sends us to Epictetus, admiring what Epictetus did indeed say nobly; yet not so nobly that his saying when his leg was broken can be compared with the marvellous works of Jesus, which Celsus disbelieves, and with his words. For these were spoken with divine power, and to this day they convert not only some of the simpler folk but also many of the more intelligent.

choices.choice: The tale of the farmer’s ox and of a sacrifice to Heracles offered with curses is probably the rite at Lindos on Rhodes known from later tradition; Origen names no source, so none is cited inline. Asclepius was discussed earlier in this work (Book 3). Celsus’s phrase ὁσίῳ χρησάμενον πνεύματι is set in quotation marks; καλῶς βεβιωκέναι (‘lived a good life’) is Origen’s gloss on it. θαυμάζω δὲ εἰ μή is taken as ‘I should be surprised if ... did not’; the colon after ἐνετύγχανεν in the staged text is ignored. ‘The good state’ (ἡ καλὴ πολιτεία) is Plato’s ideal city, from which the imitative poet is sent away (Republic 398a; Homer is criticized at 377d–383c and dismissed again at 607a). The usual tradition names the Cypriot tyrant Nicocreon (Diogenes Laertius 9.59); Origen’s text has Aristocreon, kept as written. ‘Turn to God’ renders ἐπιστρέφοντας used absolutely in its Christian sense of conversion; ‘to God’ is implied, not written. μονογενές rendered ‘the only thing’. Review: καὶ Κέλσος (‘Celsus too’) restored. διὰ τὸ ... λελέχθαι is causal and now opens its own sentence (‘For these were spoken with divine power’); the inferred ‘therefore’ and the supplied ‘to God’ were removed, and ἐπιστρέφοντας is rendered ‘convert’. Republic 607a, where Homer himself is shut out, is added beside 398a.
θαυμάσας aorist: 'does he admire' -> 'did he admire'; ὁμολογουμένως moved inside Celsus's quoted words
μονογενὲς ... θαυμαζόμενον: 'the only thing ... to admire' -> 'the one thing ... that the Greeks know and admire'
διὰ τό causal clause: removed inferred 'therefore' and supplied 'to God'; ἐπιστρέφοντας -> 'convert'
